newsitem.title: USA: Fast-growing Florida could be headed for disaster.
newsitem.headline: Fast-growing Florida could be headed for disaster.

text.p: Florida, having reaped the benefits of a population explosion spurred by abundant sunshine and low taxes, is facing a demographic disaster as seen in a shortage of schools, prisons and a crime epidemic.
"Florida is one of the fastest growing areas on earth. Faster than India, China or Japan," said demographer Leon Bouvier, a founder of Floridians for a Sustainable Growth.

State government has gone to great lengths to say it is "managing growth," but Florida's population will swell sixfold to 95 million through the end of the next century if all the permitted growth takes place, according to Bouvier, author of "Florida in the 21st Century -- The Challenge of Growth."

Florida grows by an average 750 people a day, according to census figures. And, on average, every day sees 450 acres (180 hectares) of forest land leveled, 328 acres (132 hectares) of farmland developed and an additional 110,000 gallons (416,000 litres) of water consumed.
Since the late 1860s, when doctors first began sending patients to Florida for their health, population growth has been the driving force in Florida's economy.
The benefits of that growth peaked in the 1960s with a space program drawing hi-tech industry and Walt Disney World spurring a tourist boom, experts say.
By the 1970s, people began seeing negative impacts, with crime soaring and the quality of education declining. But in the quarter century since then, no one has been able to put the brakes on.
"Our growth management system in Florida is a dismal failure," said Clay Henderson, president of the Florida Audubon Society. "We should call it the Urban Sprawl Liberation Act."
As in California and other sunbelt states, growth is spurred by warm winter weather and foreign immigration.

Only 13 percent of Florida's growth can be attributed to birth rate. Another 30 percent comes from legal foreign immigration. The largest share -- 50 percent -- comes from domestic immigration. And that, Henderson said, is a problem of the state's own making.
"Since the 1950s we've had it written into the state constitution that there would be no estate tax and no income tax," he said. "We've made this a haven for tax refugees from northern states."
The effects of growth, coupled with low taxes, is dramatically illustrated by Harry Singletary, secretary of the state's Department of Corrections.

"I spend a lot of time in prisons, and I feel very comfortable in Florida," Singletary said. "Florida itself is a big prison. There's more wrought iron bars on homes in Florida than in prisons. You go to school or to the supermarket, there's always an off-duty police officer standing guard."

Florida's prison budget is $1 billion a year for operations alone. The state needs to spend another billion over the next five years on construction to keep pace with the swelling prison population, officials said.

Seventy percent of Florida's prison inmate population is functionally illiterate. And yet the state legislature is expected to decide this year whether it can afford to give every school student a textbook, said Bouvier.
"It's clear, our education system from kindergarten through graduate school is slipping fast," he said. "We simply cannot even build enough schools to keep up with our population growth."
No one seems to offer any easy solutions.

"Where you've got to get to in Florida is that nobody moves in unless somebody moves out," said Peter Kostmayer, head of Zero Population Growth. "Of course, that's hard to accomplish because people don't like the idea of government telling them what to do."
